title: Voltage divider
probe1: The middle row, where the two resistors meet
notes: probe1_row is a placeholder until docs/HARDWARE.md lists the real probe rows.

mistakes.hint: The middle voltage is much lower than half of 5 volts. How the voltage splits depends on the sizes of the two resistors. Are they really the same size?
mistakes.explain: The bottom resistor is 1k (brown-black-red) instead of 10k (brown-black-orange). With 10k on top and 1k on the bottom, the middle gets only 1/11 of 5 volts, about 0.45 V. Use a 10k on the bottom too, so both match and the middle reads 2.5 V.

mini_lesson.title: Resistors share the voltage
mini_lesson.idea: Two resistors in a line share the voltage, like friends sharing a pizza. The bigger resistor gets the bigger share, just like the hungrier friend gets more slices. If both resistors are the same size, each one gets exactly half.
mini_lesson.question: The top resistor is 10k and the bottom one is 1k. Which one gets more of the voltage?
mini_lesson.why: The bigger resistor always gets the bigger share of the voltage.

mistakes.description: Measuring row not connected to the middle, so the number jumps
mistakes.hint: The middle voltage keeps jumping around. That happens when the measuring row is not touching anything. Check the measuring row.
mistakes.explain: The measuring row is not connected to the middle, where the two resistors meet, so it measures nothing and the number drifts. Move the wire so the measuring row connects to the middle. The lit row shows the measuring row.

mini_lesson.title: Measure only what you touch
mini_lesson.idea: A measuring wire tells you the voltage of whatever it touches. If it touches nothing, it picks up random noise, like a radio stuck between stations. That noise makes the number jump around.
mini_lesson.question: Why would a voltage number keep jumping around?
options: The measuring row is not touching anything
The power supply is almost empty
mini_lesson.why: A wire that touches nothing picks up random noise instead of a real voltage.
